hints: Focus on what free-radical substitution actually does, one H on ethane is swapped for one Br, so think about what the main two products must be.
Remember termination steps join two radicals together, so ask yourself what happens if two ethyl radicals, $\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\cdot$, meet each other.
Check whether any $\text{H}\cdot$ radicals ever exist to make $\text{H}_2$, the propagation step makes $\text{HBr}$ directly, not free H atoms.
walkthrough:
**Recall the overall substitution**

Think simple first. One hydrogen of ethane is replaced by bromine. That gives the two expected products.

$$\text{C}_2\text{H}_6 + \text{Br}_2 \rightarrow \text{C}_2\text{H}_5\text{Br} + \text{HBr}$$
So hydrogen bromide, substance 3, is definitely formed.

**Look at the propagation in detail**

The chain works with $\text{Br}\cdot$ and ethyl radicals, not $\text{H}\cdot$.

$$\text{Br}\cdot + \text{C}_2\text{H}_6 \rightarrow \text{C}_2\text{H}_5\cdot + \text{HBr}$$
$$\text{C}_2\text{H}_5\cdot + \text{Br}_2 \rightarrow \text{C}_2\text{H}_5\text{Br} + \text{Br}\cdot$$
Notice hydrogen leaves as $\text{HBr}$ straight away. No free hydrogen atoms are made, so $\text{H}_2$ cannot form this way.

**Do not forget termination**

In termination, any two radicals can combine. Most students forget this, but it gives extra minor products.

$$\text{C}_2\text{H}_5\cdot + \text{C}_2\text{H}_5\cdot \rightarrow \text{C}_4\text{H}_{10}$$
Two ethyl radicals joining gives butane, substance 1. So butane is a possible trace product.

**Put it together**

Substance 1 (butane) is possible by radical combination. Substance 3 (hydrogen bromide) is the main co-product. Substance 2 (hydrogen) has no route to form. That leaves 1 and 3 only.

options.A: Includes hydrogen as well as butane and hydrogen bromide. Hydrogen, $\text{H}_2$, would need $\text{H}\cdot + \text{H}\cdot$ combination, but $\text{H}\cdot$ radicals are not formed in this mechanism. Hydrogen is abstracted directly as $\text{HBr}$.
options.B: Includes butane and hydrogen but misses the key product. Hydrogen bromide is always formed in the propagation step when $\text{Br}\cdot$ abstracts H from ethane, while $\text{H}_2$ is not formed at all.
options.C: Correct. $\text{HBr}$ is the normal propagation product from $\text{Br}\cdot + \text{C}_2\text{H}_6 \rightarrow \text{C}_2\text{H}_5\cdot + \text{HBr}$, and butane, $\text{C}_4\text{H}_{10}$, is possible by termination $\text{C}_2\text{H}_5\cdot + \text{C}_2\text{H}_5\cdot \rightarrow \text{C}_4\text{H}_{10}$. No route gives $\text{H}_2$.
options.D: Includes hydrogen bromide correctly but swaps butane for hydrogen. Butane is possible by ethyl radical combination, whereas hydrogen is impossible because free $\text{H}\cdot$ radicals do not occur in alkane bromination.
